en: [Subhāsitapajjasaṅgaha] [p.
76] What can we say of the bliss of the exquisite beauty of every limb belonging to those young women?

Even though you know it, there is indeed nothing that can protect you from the touch of fear regarding your own views. O child with eyes like a lotus, you are exceedingly difficult for the eyes of young men to withstand;
seized by the hand of the God of Love, you are like an irresistible sword-blade.
By his gaze, which was as salty as the shimmering spray of water from the rays of the moon,
my hair became moist as if sprinkled by moonstones; likewise,
I was made to dance upon the stage of the theater of new love.
O Mother! My very heart is not astonished that it forgets [all else].

(Subhāṣitapaddhati-Saṃgraha 4) The glance of the eyes of those with deer-like eyes produces a fever even though it consists of nectar; it bewilders even though it is life-giving; it pierces the mind even though it is soft. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-Saṃgraha 5)
The side-long glances of noble women, exceedingly long and crooked, delude the minds of people like serpents red with anger and black with poison, whose venom is irresistible and cruel.
They cannot endure the good fortune of others, nor do they ever grant a pleasant look. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-Saṃgraha 6)

Alas! Her virtues steal away life in separation; they are like wicked men. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-Padyasaṃgraha 7) Couples become angry when their own body parts fail to provide pleasure for the beloved, yet they are even more envious when other things provide such pleasure. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-Padyasaṃgraha 8)

How can there be happiness in a state where one’s dwelling is in an improper place, one’s bed is uneven, one stumbles at every word, one’s eyes are fixed upon Varatta, and passion is concealed? When the suffering of separation from a beloved person is heard, it gives rise to joy. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-Saṃgraha 9)

In happiness there is suffering; alas, the course of love is treacherous! (Subhāṣitapaddhati-Saṃgraha 10) The tongue of those who call even that "love" for which the inner essence consists of the haughty, the shameless, and the wicked, even their tongue feels ashamed. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-Saṃgraha 11)
She is a true friend who has resided in your heart this very moment;
Alas! O heart, you who lack courage, you shall obtain hundreds of thousands of miseries.
Who indeed would be bound by love for women with downcast eyes, even in the dwellings that are the abodes of a hundred beloveds—those places which resemble the twilight glow and are cherished by men?
Even an offense brings supreme joy to a beloved person; even the smoke from fragrant substances greatly steals away the heart's peace. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-Saṃgraha 15)
Even the speech of the ill-mannered brings joy to those who possess sovereignty and prosperity; even a cowardly king—does he not indeed conquer the world in battle?
That alone is wealth which is in hand, and that alone is a friend who remains constant in times of calamity.
That form wherein there are virtues, that consciousness wherein there is Dharma—such a one is a source of happiness, like a supreme and unprecedented treasure, or like a pain removed;
O cursed Fate, though he be near, why indeed have you made him far from me? (Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 17–18)
Even though he stands far away, he alone dwells in my heart; like a cloud over a pond, he is there, while what need is there for other new lotuses?
When the night had passed, he was forbidden by his attendants from entering the presence of the angry Yama.

For a girl of noble family, modesty is her elder sister. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-Saṃgraha 20) The radiance of the glance of that maiden as she walks—extremely innocent, charming, and tremulous, with rolling eyes—is especially difficult to endure, like a young serpent. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-Saṃgraha 21)
It is indeed true that she alone is my delight, for even my mind, with its eyes turned upward, strikes her; yet that wretched Flower-Arrowed One (Kāma) strikes me with his uneven arrows.
Even today, that bodiless one remains truly ashamed of his skill in archery.
It is said that there are three hundred million worlds, and furthermore, five arrows. O gentle one!
Having extracted the essence of the nectar from the moon, the Creator fashioned your face;
it is for this reason that people call its surface a "spot. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 23–24)
In the absence of those virtues, there is longing; in their remembrance, a fever of burning;
when seen, a state of trembling and palpitating; but when the beloved has met, there is some indescribable happiness.
(Subhāṣitapaddhati-Saṃgraha 25) I have seen her face with its affectionate eyes, beautiful with the grace of modesty.
Indeed, this hand, which binds the hair-knot upon the lotus of the head, steals [the heart] from the hearts of even the steadfast.

(Subhāṣitapaddhati-Saṃgraha 26) This left hand, which has attained its purpose through the right eye, throbs; how indeed can it be called "left" for you who have obtained that which is difficult to find? (Subhāṣitapaddhati-Saṃgraha 27)

Form is the object of the eyes, qualities of the mind, the range of sight for the feet, the basis for conversation, and the bond for every limb; what more can we say of it? (Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 28)
"Remember me"—this is merely an external expression of love; "May it be well with me"—this does not hold true;
"Do not despair"—this contradicts actual experience. What can I say here?
[It is] a binding of the eyes, a wandering of the mind, a delusion caused by pain. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 29)

The beauty of form belonging to those who are ignorant and difficult to perceive is like that of a wicked person. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 30) Victory to the abundance of childhood and love in this world—both possessing speech like nectar, never ceasing, never satiated, and free from the agitation of failed undertakings. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 31)
Even without the union with the Gaṅgā, the ocean remains an ocean;
but tell me, where could the Gaṅgā find rest for even a moment without him?
She is like a housewife, like the goddess Lakṣmī, like a great treasure, like nectar, and like a pure pearl.
Wherever there is a house, they consider that alone to be a forest;
(33) for virtuous women are a mine of virtues and an ornament of the entire earth, such that even faults, when placed within them, are transformed into the form of virtues. (34)
To those noble women, whose natural majesty is true and cannot be attained by others—
for whom even faults incurred through opposition do not disturb the mind—
to those female ascetics who have practiced celibacy throughout their entire lives, I offer salutations. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-Saṃgraha 35)

For those who do not experience even for a moment the torment of being crushed, weighed, cut, and pierced—let even the three worlds perform the gleaning for them. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 36) Even if it is split and squeezed, the stalk of the *picchula* reed does not truly lose its sweetness. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 37)

A woman becomes infatuated with favor and possesses her own radiance; however, a virtuous man does not exist without the moon, nor is there night without the moon, nor is there day without the sun. (Subhāṣitapadyasaṃgraha 38) "O Mother! I consider that what else could be difficult for you to do for my sake?"
"O Mother! It is said that even though you were but a child, you were placed in the midst of the virtuous.

When they see you—who have committed an offense—with joy, and I with embarrassment, do not look again toward my feet in anger, O Mother, for my heart is not capable [of such resentment]! (Subhāṣitapaddhati-Padyasaṃgraha 39–40)
With eyes unsteady from craving, with hands grasping the hem of his garment in exhaustion,

attached to suffering, bewildered by the Dharma, yet at ease in your happiness— [O Lord,] you are the gambling match for riches, the calamity for virtues, and the adversary of favors. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-Padyasaṃgraha 41)

The examination of objects uproots love along with its very foundation. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 42) Modesty and family honor are the two door-panels; when these are shattered within the hearts of men, suffering enters suddenly and unimpeded. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 43)
The sages recognize that the true form of modesty belongs to love, to a young woman, to wealth, to a rain-cloud, to the Supreme Self, and to the mind. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-Padyasaṃgraha 44)

The majesty of holy places, of great men, of jewels, of lineages, and of medicinal herbs, as well as that of great rivers, remains far removed from the corruption of time. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-Saṃgraha 45) A city filled with great festivals is empty of true prosperity; a mind full of great undertakings is empty of wisdom. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-Saṃgraha 45)
This arrow, which has been driven into my heart by misfortune, is a triple-pointed shaft.

(Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 46) A man deprived of wealth, a household lacking a wife, a king fallen from his royal status, and a woman whose youth has passed—these do not regain even their former splendor. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 47)
The womb of the wealthy is a treasury of pride; for the destitute, it is a source of charity and virtue;
but for ascetics, that belly is like deadly halāhala poison disguised as nectar.
O most wretched one, you are such a person, since even when a single virtue is perceived in you... [Subhāṣitapaddhati-Saṃgraha 48]
O Lord! Though Your virtues are indeed immeasurable, You bear the face of both the moon and the fire.
(49) I shall not grasp Your virtues; for while grasping both [the moon and the fire] would be impossible for you, it would be an excessive delusion for me to grasp them. (50)
Having sent forth his broad bracelets like messengers into the darkness of battle, he pursued the fortune of his enemies;
having seized those bracelets, he was one who had captured the bracelets of his foes. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-Padyasaṃgraha 51) *gahiyacāvalayā* means "one who has seized the bracelets of his enemies."
O King! Being red yourself, you surely display a resemblance to the clouds.
O cloud! Having raised yourself up in the sky, even your thundering is fitting;
for you proceed to sprinkle with water the world that was about to be consumed by the thunderbolt.
Even if a wealthy man’s son should somehow come within the range of his vision without being disciplined,

women who are obsessed with affection for their children do not consider even that suffering to be anything other than happiness— regardless of nectar, the moon, moonlight, or sandalwood paste. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-Saṃgraha 54)
Blessed indeed are those noble women who have utterly destroyed the power of delusion,
for they do not even look upon the faces of others, which are adorned with wide-open frowns, though those faces may be fondled by other children. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 55–56)
On the days of the spring festival, the young girls sing of nothing but the cluster of flowers beginning with pearls and jasmine;
they do not even mention the *nōmāliyā* flower.
[The Lord is] the majesty of the king of warriors, the source of the *sumanta* [mantras], and the bow of the flower-arrowed god of love.
And likewise, O great serpent, do not turn back from what has been done!
Rain constantly, give gifts, and travel by way of the mind-delighting path.
O you who are skillful in deeds and agile! O noble one, if you desire happiness—then [these things] increase together with Kṛṣṇa:
the fear of death for enemies, the heart’s desire of kinsmen, the joy of the cowherd, and the sentiment of love for the cowherdesses. (Subhāṣitapadyasaṃgraha 59–60)
Even when enraged, a good person bestows the excellence of nectar and other such things; whereas a wicked person, however, brings about the misfortune of even fire and other such elements.

What can we say of the greatness of the great rivers, by the power of whose waters [the earth is sustained]? (Subhāṣitapaddhati-Saṃgraha 61) [The greatness of the great rivers is such that]... by the majesty of whose waters... [the world is sustained].
An undertaking that results in the fruit of liberation arises; even prosperity becomes a cow of plenty.

Of what use are those riches which are never utilized, being like the water in a well belonging to a *caṇḍāla*—even when they have somehow reached those who are worthy recipients? (Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 62)
What can we say of those wicked people who have abandoned the sustenance of their own kin?
For them, happiness and suffering are cast aside by both the miserable and the fortunate alike.
(Subhāṣitapaddhati-Padyasaṃgraha 63) Charity, the uplifting of the distressed, listening to the scriptures, and pilgrimages to sacred sites.
Devotion to the Teaching is the fruit-bearing excellence of the tree that is human birth. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 64) What can even that achieve which is not watered by the essence of sincerity?
For a person, like a clod of earth, breaks apart and crumbles away. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 65)
For those whose wealth has vanished, charity is the gift; for those whose youth is worn away by old age, marriage is the gift;
for those whose lives are headed toward death, the Dharma is the gift; and for those in the autumn season, agricultural labor is the gift.
But for women, their own unseparated self alone is the entirety of happiness. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 66)
Those who desire happiness only for themselves are rare indeed.
Homage to those whose character is like the Mūga mountain: even when the clouds of Puṣkala rain down for a long time, they do not leak even a little of their teacher’s nectar-like essence.
Just as the rainy season finds glory with a girdle of water-bearing clouds,
and the spring with the jasmine, so does a man find glory with a wife who is a ground for the forest of virtues.
Indeed, even faults become virtues where love alone prevails.
It is said that even base metals become gold where there is the philosopher’s stone;
yet for some, even the days spent with a lotus pond bring only long-lasting torment,
and in their company, even a friend withdraws his life along with one's own.
Now that even the wife of a virtuous man has been ruined, and the storehouse of household goods emptied, men remain like fish in shallow water. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-Paryāya-saṃgraha 72, p.
The excellence of union with a beloved shines forth most intensely through separation;
the greatness of cool waters is made manifest by the summer heat.
Pride is the ornament of virtues, sleep is the ornament of those who have studied, and calamity is the ornament of the instructions of one's gurus.
Generosity is the most beautiful of riches; greed is the destroyer of happiness.

(Subhāṣitapaddhati-Saṃgraha 75) One who is full of merit smiles joyfully upon meeting others from foreign lands, while one devoid of merit wanders aimlessly within the walls of his own home. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-Saṃgraha 76)

Bound tightly and held in secret, even after being buried in a pit and cut into pieces by the miser, how was Fortune not released? [By those free from] envy, dejection, fear, anger, greed, ignorance, pride, and lust. (Subhāṣitapadyasaṃgraha 77) [With envy, dejection, fear, anger, greed, ignorance, pride, and lust.]
Multitudes of living beings are made to dance upon the reed-pipes of saṃsāra. O daughter!
What can those possessed of virtues do for a master who does not recognize the excellence of their qualities?
A pearl does not fetch its price when it is worn as an ornament by a Pulinda hunter.
What is difficult to obtain? Instruction. What is far away? That which is elevated by the mind.
What is delightful? That in which there is joy. What is desolate? Where there is no virtuous friend.
Here, knowledge is measured by the throat [the depth of one's learning], and pride is measured by love; this is beneficial for the heart.

Knowledge is the knowledge of one’s own seat; charity is the measure of one’s own wealth. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 81) Indeed, modesty, virtue, and the instruction of elders remain in the heart of people as long as the burning of the stomach-fire does not awaken. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 82)
What can we say of that fire of separation, which burns the body even while it is moist with affection—a fire for which even sandalwood paste acts as fuel? O moon-faced one!
O you whose speech is like nectar! O you with eyes like blue lotuses! O you with thighs like the trunks of plantain trees! Subhāṣitapaddhati-Padyasaṃgraha 83.
Even though you were placed in her heart, how indeed could she find you there when her heart was devastated by separation?
(Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 84) O moon-faced one! By your virtues and even by your modesty, you alone are surely highly esteemed;
for even those [virtues], when taken up by you, become like nectar, whereas they are like poison to those devoid of merit. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 85)

Aha-ha! This great human birth of the fool has been plundered by the thieves of the sense-objects, like the consumption of a blind merchant's wealth by wayward children. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-Saṃgraha 86) [p.

O fish, how could that river—whose course was crooked and which even left its net behind—have died, deprived of you, O fool? Having burned away the constant misery of separation, as if it were the state of being a co-wife... [Subhāṣitapaddhati-Saṃgraha 87]... having burned away the state of being a co-wife.
Now that fate has been determined, I experience neither sorrow nor joy.

(Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 88) Even though he has attained the glory of lordship, even though he is worthy of being honored by you, and even though he is a pearl among the [ocean’s] waves, the moon does not attain purity due to the fault of his association with the dull-witted (the ocean). (Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 89)

Aha! This is the work of Fate, which, even when one has performed the action oneself, dictates that one must lament like a lover for a remedy that no longer exists—those very things which, once cast far away, still burn the person even from a distance. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 90)
O Rāghava, O Lord! For the wise, it is not fitting to dwell in those sense-objects. (Subhāṣitapaddhati-saṃgraha 91)
